content: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is a common medical condition caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel in the wrist. The carpal tunnel is a narrow passageway formed by bones and ligaments at the base of the hand that protects the median nerve and tendons. When this nerve is compressed or pinched, it can lead to symptoms such as pain, numbness, tingling, and weakness in the hand and fingers, particularly affecting the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring finger. The pathophysiology of CTS involves increased pressure within the carpal tunnel leading to nerve ischemia and impaired nerve conduction. Major risk factors include repetitive hand and wrist movements, wrist anatomy, pregnancy, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and occupational activities involving prolonged wrist flexion or extension. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by nerve conduction studies and electromyography to assess nerve function. Management of CTS ranges from conservative measures such as wrist splinting, activity modification, and anti-inflammatory medications, to surgical release of the transverse carpal ligament in more severe cases. Ergonomic interventions and lifestyle modifications can reduce symptoms and prevent progression. Early recognition and treatment are important to prevent permanent nerve damage. Although commonly called by the abbreviation CTS, related terms include median nerve entrapment neuropathy and nerve compression syndrome of the wrist. Limitations in knowledge include variability in individual responses to treatment and the multifactorial nature of symptoms. Safety considerations involve ensuring accurate diagnosis to exclude other conditions and weighing risks versus benefits of surgical intervention. This module provides evidence-based consumer health education ideal for patient understanding and clinical support.

chunk_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Carpal Tunnel
content: The carpal tunnel is a narrow, rigid passageway on the palm side of the wrist composed of carpal bones and the transverse carpal ligament. The median nerve and nine flexor tendons pass through this tunnel. The median nerve provides sensation to the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring fingers, and controls some thumb muscles.

chunk_title: Causes and Risk Factors of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
content: CTS occurs when pressure within the carpal tunnel increases, compressing the median nerve. Causes include repetitive hand or wrist movements, wrist injuries, arthritis, fluid retention during pregnancy, diabetes, obesity, hypothyroidism, and anatomical variations. Occupational risk factors include jobs requiring long periods of wrist flexion or forceful gripping.

content: Common symptoms include numbness, tingling, burning sensation, pain especially at night, and weakness in the affected hand. Symptoms typically affect the thumb, index, middle, and half of the ring fingers. Activities such as holding a phone or steering wheel can worsen symptoms.

content: Diagnosis of CTS is primarily clinical based on history and physical examination. Provocative tests such as Tinel's sign and Phalen maneuver help identify median nerve irritation. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG) can confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and exclude other conditions.

content: Initial treatment includes wrist splinting (especially at night), activity modification to reduce repetitive wrist use, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and corticosteroid injections. Physical therapy techniques and ergonomics can also provide symptom relief.

content: For moderate to severe or persistent CTS, surgical decompression of the carpal tunnel by cutting the transverse carpal ligament may be recommended. Surgery typically results in symptom relief and prevents further nerve damage. Risks include infection, nerve injury, and scar tenderness.

content: Preventive measures include ergonomic adjustments such as maintaining neutral wrist positions during work, taking regular breaks, strengthening hand muscles, and managing underlying health conditions like diabetes. Avoiding repetitive stress and forceful grips helps reduce risk.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Untreated CTS can lead to permanent nerve damage, muscle wasting of the thumb, and loss of hand function. Most individuals improve with early treatment, but prognosis depends on symptom duration and severity at diagnosis.

chunk_title: Common Misconceptions About Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
content: Some believe CTS only affects office workers or is caused solely by computer use, which is incorrect. Symptoms can mimic other nerve or musculoskeletal conditions. Surgery is not always required and conservative treatments are effective for many.

chunk_title: Safety and When to Seek Medical Advice
content: If symptoms are severe, increasing, or associated with muscle weakness, medical evaluation is essential. Early diagnosis reduces risks of permanent damage. Self-treatment should not delay seeking professional care if symptoms persist.
